chunks.text: Jamun (Syzygium cumini), also called the Java plum or black plum, is an evergreen tree in the myrtle family Myrtaceae, native to the Indian subcontinent — India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and the Andaman Islands — and extending through Southeast Asia into Indonesia and Hainan in southern China; it has since been introduced to Queensland, Florida and various Pacific territories. The tree can reach 30 metres and live over a century, with rough dark grey bark that lightens and smooths higher up the trunk. Young leaves are pinkish, maturing to glossy dark green with yellow midribs, and small fragrant flowers appear in March-April. The oblong fruit ripens from green through pink and crimson to black, and has a distinctive sweet, sourish and astringent taste; it is roughly 83% water and 16% carbohydrate, providing about 60 calories per 100 grams.

chunks.source: Wikipedia — Syzygium cumini (uses, ecology and cultural significance)
chunks.text: Jamun fruit is eaten fresh or made into sauces, jams, juices, jellies, sorbets and syrups such as kala khatta, and has a long history of traditional use, including historical references to its use for spleen ailments; it is also popularly associated with traditional home remedies related to blood sugar, though the Wikipedia article does not detail clinical evidence for this. Its timber, once kiln-dried, resists water and has been used for railway sleepers, well linings, bullock-cart wheels, doors and windows, although its hardness makes it difficult to work. The fruit attracts birds, jackals, civets and fruit bats that disperse its seeds, but the tree's fast growth and prolific seeding have made it invasive in Florida, South Africa, the Caribbean, Hawaii and parts of Oceania. Buddhist tradition places one of the Buddha's early childhood meditative experiences under a jamun (jambu) tree, and in Hindu tradition the fruit is associated with Krishna; in Maharashtra its leaves are used in wedding decorations.
